This report analyzes 1,465 Amazon India products across multiple categories. After data cleaning, 1,462 products with complete pricing, rating, and discount data form the analytical base. The dataset spans prices from ₹39 to ₹139,900, with discount percentages ranging from 0% to 94%.

Key Headline: The catalog is in generally strong shape — 75.9% of products earn a rating of 4.0 or above. However, the correlation between discount depth and customer satisfaction is effectively zero (r=-0.156), meaning deeper discounts do not translate into higher ratings. Margins are being sacrificed without a measurable satisfaction payoff.

3. Pricing & Discount Strategy Analysis

This is the most strategically critical section. Management needs to understand whether discounts are driving satisfaction or simply eroding margin.

3.1 Discount–Rating Correlation

Finding: The Pearson correlation between discount percentage and customer rating is r = -0.156 (p = 0.0000). This is a negligible negative correlation — deeper discounts do not produce higher ratings. In fact, there is a very slight tendency for heavily discounted products to have marginally lower ratings, possibly reflecting lower perceived quality at steeper markdowns.

3.2 Discount–Engagement Correlation

The correlation between discount percentage and log-transformed rating count is r = -0.106 (p = 0.0000). This indicates a weak negative relationship — discounts have a marginal effect on review volume but are far from the primary driver of engagement.

3.3 Discount Tier Analysis

Grouping products into discount tiers reveals how rating and engagement change across discount levels:

Promotional budgets should be redirected from blanket discounts toward quality improvements and targeted category-level interventions.

Insight: There is a weak positive correlation (r = 0.236) between rating and engagement volume. Products with more reviews tend to have slightly higher ratings, which may reflect either popularity-driven positivity bias or genuinely better products attracting more customers. The long-tail of low-engagement products represents an opportunity to either boost visibility or cull underperformers.

5. Review Sentiment Snapshot

A keyword-frequency analysis of review titles and content reveals the dominant themes in customer feedback. Positive sentiment keywords outnumber negative ones by a significant margin: 92.9% of matched sentiment words are positive, versus 7.1% negative.

5.1 Dominant Positive Themes

  • Value for money — "worth," "value," and "good for price" appear frequently, confirming that customers prize cost-effectiveness.
  • Product quality — "good quality," "durable," and "reliable" signal that build quality is a key satisfier.
  • Performance — "fast," "works well," and "satisfied" indicate functional performance meets expectations for most products.

5.2 Dominant Negative Themes

  • Quality failures — "poor," "cheap," and "defective" point to durability and build-quality issues in underperforming products.
  • Product not matching expectations — "disappointed," "waste," and "misleading" suggest gaps between product descriptions and actual experience.
  • Functional issues — "stopped," "not working," and "broken" indicate reliability problems, particularly in electronics and accessories.
Actionable Signal: The most common negative themes relate to product quality and expectation mismatches — not price. This reinforces the quantitative finding that discount depth does not compensate for quality shortfalls. Investing in quality control and accurate product descriptions would address the root causes of dissatisfaction more effectively than deeper discounts.

6. Strategic Recommendations

Each recommendation below is grounded in a specific data finding from this analysis.

1. Reallocate Discount Budget from Deep Markdowns to Quality Improvement

With a near-zero correlation (r = -0.156) between discount depth and customer rating, deep discounts are eroding margins without improving satisfaction. Redirect promotional spend toward supplier quality programs and product testing — the dominant negative sentiment themes ("poor," "defective," "stopped working") point to quality gaps that discounts cannot fix.

Evidence: Discount–Rating correlation r = -0.156; top negative keywords: poor, defective, stopped working.

2. Audit and Improve Low-Rated Sub-Categories

Several sub-categories fall below a 3.8 average rating — well under the catalog average of 4.10. Conduct a product-level audit in these segments to identify and remove chronically low-rated SKUs. Replace them with higher-quality alternatives or require enhanced quality verification for new listings in these categories.

Evidence: 15 sub-categories rank in the bottom tier; catalog average is 4.10 while bottom performers fall below 3.8.

3. Leverage High-Engagement Products as Category Anchors

Products with massive review counts (39,639+ ratings at the 90th percentile) are proven winners. Use these as anchor products in category merchandising — feature them prominently, cross-sell from them, and study their attributes (pricing, features, descriptions) as templates for new product selection.

Evidence: 90th percentile rating count is 39,639; top-10 most-reviewed products average 4.22 rating.

4. Adopt Tiered Discount Strategy by Price Segment

Rather than uniform discounting, align discount depth to price segment behavior. Budget products (40% avg discount) already carry deep markdowns — further reductions yield diminishing returns. For premium segments (44% avg discount), moderate discounts may attract more trial without excessive margin erosion. Set category-specific discount caps informed by the tier analysis.

Evidence: Budget segment avg discount = 40.4%; Premium = 44.2%; no rating benefit from deeper discounts.

5. Close the Expectation–Reality Gap in Product Descriptions

"Disappointed" and "misleading" are among the top negative sentiment words. This indicates product descriptions or images are setting expectations that products fail to meet. Implement description accuracy audits and add customer photo galleries to set realistic expectations, particularly in the lowest-rated sub-categories.

Evidence: "disappointed" and "misleading" rank among top negative keywords; rating–discount correlation is near-zero, confirming satisfaction is driven by expectation match, not price.

Methodology & Data Notes

  • Data source: Amazon India product catalog snapshot (Kaggle dataset, 1465 products, 16 columns).
  • Data cleaning: Currency symbols (₹) and commas removed from price/rating-count columns; percentage symbols stripped from discount field. Products with missing or malformed values in key columns were excluded, yielding 1462 valid records for analysis.
  • Category extraction: The pipe-delimited category field was split to derive top-level and sub-level categories.
  • Sentiment analysis: Keyword-matching approach applied to review titles and content. This is a high-level frequency analysis, not a machine-learning sentiment model. Results should be interpreted as directional indicators rather than precise sentiment scores.
  • Correlations: Pearson correlation coefficients reported. Rating count was log-transformed (log1p) where noted to address extreme skew.
  • Currency: All prices are in Indian Rupees (₹).
